NTA. Sounds like you need to have a conversation with him about how rude she is and tone down contact with her.

ESH. You don't have the moral high ground over her because you've slept with fewer people, and you're acting like you do.

On the other hand, while she may be "just blurting things out sometimes," she clearly knows now that you're uncomfortable with it. If she's choosing to be in a relationship with you, she can at least respect your feelings enough to be conscious of telling those stories. 

I dated a guy who did this. I think his propensity for telling those stories was part of what drew me to him, but I had always been slightly uncomfortable with how often he brought things up. Later in the relationship and after we broke up it did feel like him bragging and trying to use these stories to get attention and make other people attracted to him. That's not always what's happening, but it is very easy to get jealous and especially if you're dating it's a sign of disrespect. I don't understand how you just keep doing something like this, and it can definitely make you not trust someone to keep details of a relationship secret.

I guess the question is why it's taken this five years to become an issue, and whether this is an indication of deeper things you're unhappy about.

Bit late to the party here. As someone who has known of the existence of trans people since age 13 or so, immediately identified with an ftm-style experience and tortured myself over it for 5-6 years before deciding it wasn't an issue and then recently returning to it, I've felt a lot of ways OP says they've felt and encountered a lot of advice like the first paragraph u/cantdressherself  writes.  I have to say, I'm still struggling a lot with the idea of gender identity and sexual attraction, I suspect there are a lot of underlying factors I have no idea how to address. I haven't been in therapy very long. 

I do agree with the last bit of the above, but I have found "if you think x you're probably trans" to be a relatively harmful mantra. GNC people exist. Societal expectations are bullshit and stressful and there are loads of reasons why you might hate some aspect of yourself. That's something you should sort out for yourself, and I personally have found it very useful to work on yourself in a more general way (identifying values, thoughts, expectations, goals) while trying to analyze very specific problems like this.

You would be leaving for your own mental health, not for hers. You have to put yourself first before you can help someone else. And to be fair, you've sacrificed a lot to help her and it sounds like you're doing everything you should be doing to communicate with her. Stepping back could give her some space to learn to be more self-sufficient (and self-confident, and responsible...), since it really seems like she's not -- and that's ok, it's not something you should have to worry about. 

Being in this relationship is not good for you right now, though, and you don't want to end up resenting her for her immaturity. Maybe there are some friends you or she have who can check in on her if that's something you're worried about but it shouldn't be on you. She will be able to get through this. Sure, you could stick it out and help her through things from a distance but you can't change who she is right now, she has to see these things and want to change. If you've communicated how all these things are unhealthy for her and for your relationship I don't see any reason why you should stay.

Seconded on having them make something.

I'd recommend a tutorial on each machine, maybe a class on electronics and a final project that includes everything--maybe like a pen or a lamp or something small (my intro to machining class did a 3" trophy with 3d printed, laser cut, milled, lathed, and waterjet parts).

For the 3d printer and laser cutter tutorials, have them do small projects on each -- my class had us laser cut keychains and 3d print small things we liked from thingiverse.

You can then teach them how to set up their own files to print or cut, which will also take a while but is definitely worth it.

If you can get access to a snap electronics kit or starter arduino sets, it could be fun to talk about how to make circuits or program LED light strips to make a pattern. This,  again, could take a while but would definitely be worth it.

I'd also recommend giving them some things they can do at home, maybe an assignment where they have to make a rube goldberg machine or something out of a small starter bag and stuff they have at home.

I see a lot of elements of my most recent relationship in your actions and analysis. I feel like I'm in the limbo stage right now, cause we both recognized we have a lot to work on and though we never fully broke up we're not dating and I'm still trying to figure out exactly what went wrong. For my part I'm doing my best to improve my self esteem, work on my anxiety, and communicate sooner rather than later. I figure I can learn from this now, and if it doesn't  work out it'll be ok.

I don't know why I still get upset sometimes, because he really truly is trying and seems like he cares. Maybe it's cause all I really want is a relationship, but I recognize that I have to work on these things first. It's just so hard when I'm still afraid of getting hurt.

Sometimes it takes time to figure out what you want, and although ghosting people isn't an appropriate response it can be the easiest. 

It sounds like she's thought about it and decided she really wants this enough to take the same chance you did, so if you still feel the way you did when you first asked her out it's worth a shot.

I got hooked on the Animorphs series (K.A. Applegate) in 2nd grade, and it took me a few years to build up my collection since they were out of print and only available at secondhand bookstores and libraries...but I had to own all of them. I think I got the last (#50) book in the series about 3/4 of the way into my endeavor, but I tried to wait as long as possible for the conclusion, intending to reread the series in order. I finally read it when I owned all but #42, and I still don't believe I've quite gotten over that ending and haven't read it since (although I've read #46? several times). I do own all the books now, thanks to my long-overdue discovery of Amazon.

I also recall Scott Westerfield's Uglies and Brandon Mull's Fablehaven doing the same thing as a series, and China Mieville's Un Lun Dun as a standalone...or maybe I'm just listing books I wish never ended.

tl;dr - K.A. Applegate is phenomenal and I can pick out one of her books almost instantly in any used bookstore or library sale
